title: Configuration as code for endpoints
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Treat endpoint configuration as versioned, reviewable code: define policies as JSON, store them in Git, and deploy them to Intune through Graph with idempotent import scripts.
objectives: Explain why endpoint configuration should be declarative, versioned code
Export an existing Intune policy as JSON via Graph
Store policy definitions in Git and review changes through pull requests
Write an idempotent import that creates or updates a policy by name
Separate environment-specific values from policy templates
Understand the IntuneCM / community tooling landscape for config as code

quiz.q: What is the core principle of configuration as code for endpoints?
options: Define configuration declaratively in versioned files and deploy it through automation
quiz.why: Config as code means the desired state lives in declarative, version-controlled files that are deployed by automation, giving you review, history, rollback, and repeatability.

quiz.q: Why export Intune policies to JSON and keep them in Git?
options: JSON runs faster than the portal
You get change history, peer review via pull requests, and reliable rollback
quiz.why: Versioning policy JSON in Git gives you a diffable audit trail, code review through pull requests, and the ability to roll back to a known-good state.

quiz.q: What makes an import script idempotent when applying a policy?
options: It checks whether a policy of that name exists and updates it, otherwise creates it
It always creates a new policy each run
It only runs once per tenant
quiz.why: An idempotent import is safe to re-run: it looks up the policy by a stable key (like displayName), updating if present and creating if absent, so repeated runs converge on the same state.

quiz.q: How should environment-specific values (tenant, group ids) be handled in config as code?
options: Hard-code them in each policy file
Keep them in separate parameter/variable files and inject at deploy time
Store them inside the policy displayName
quiz.why: Separating environment values from policy templates lets the same template deploy to dev and prod by swapping a parameter file, avoiding copy-paste drift.

quiz.q: Name one Graph endpoint family you would call to manage Intune device configuration profiles as code.
quiz.answer: deviceManagement/deviceConfigurations (or the settings-catalog configurationPolicies and deviceCompliancePolicies endpoints) under https://graph.microsoft.com.
quiz.why: These endpoints expose Intune configuration and compliance policies as resources you can GET to export and POST/PATCH to import, which is what config-as-code tooling drives.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why is a pull request review valuable for an Intune policy change?
quiz.answer: A reviewer can see the exact JSON diff before it reaches devices, catching mistakes like an over-broad assignment or a wrong setting before they affect the fleet.
quiz.why: Policy changes are high blast-radius; reviewing the diff in a pull request applies the same safety net to configuration that teams already apply to code.

body_markdown:
## Why configuration should be code

Clicking through the Intune portal works for one device, once. It does not scale, it leaves no history, and a wrong click can hit thousands of endpoints. **Configuration as code** treats your **desired state** as declarative files — JSON policy definitions — kept in **Git** and deployed by automation. You gain a diffable **audit trail**, **peer review** through pull requests, and **rollback** to any prior commit.

The mental model: the repo is the source of truth, and Intune is just the runtime that the repo deploys to.

## Export what you already have

Start by capturing your current state. Graph exposes configuration profiles as resources you can `GET` and serialise to JSON.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All'

$policies = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies' |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty value

foreach ($p in $policies) {
    $safe = $p.name -replace '[^\w\-]', '_'
    $p | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content ".\policies\$safe.json" -Encoding UTF8
}
```

Commit that `policies` folder to Git. You now have a baseline you can diff against forever.

## Idempotent import: create or update by name

The heart of config as code is an import that is **safe to re-run**. It looks the policy up by a stable key — usually `displayName` or `name` — then **updates** it if it exists and **creates** it if it does not.

```powershell
function Import-IntunePolicy {
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]
    param([Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Path)

    $def  = Get-Content $Path -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
    $base = 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies'

    $existing = (Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
        -Uri "$base?`$filter=name eq '$($def.name)'").value

    if ($existing) {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($def.name, 'Update policy')) {
            Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method PATCH `
                -Uri "$base/$($existing[0].id)" -Body ($def | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
        }
    }
    else {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($def.name, 'Create policy')) {
            Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST `
                -Uri $base -Body ($def | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
        }
    }
}
```

Run it twice; the second run changes nothing. That is the property you want.

## Separate templates from environment values

Never hard-code tenant or group ids inside a policy template. Keep them in a **parameter file** per environment and inject at deploy time, so the *same* template promotes from **dev** to **prod** by swapping one file.

```powershell
$env = Get-Content '.\envs\prod.json' -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
$template = (Get-Content '.\templates\baseline.json' -Raw) `
    -replace '{{TargetGroupId}}', $env.TargetGroupId
```

## The tooling landscape

You can write your own importer, or stand on community tooling. Projects like the **IntuneCM** family and Microsoft's own samples wrap this export/import/assign loop with backup and reporting. Whatever you use, the principles are identical: declarative files, Git review, idempotent deploy.

## Your task

Build a minimal config-as-code pipeline by hand. Export at least two Intune **configurationPolicies** to JSON and commit them. Write an idempotent `Import-IntunePolicy` function (create-or-update by name, with `SupportsShouldProcess`). Move one environment-specific value — a target group id — out of the template into a per-environment JSON file and inject it at deploy time. Demonstrate a re-run that reports *no changes* the second time, and capture the `-WhatIf` output as proof of a safe dry run.

slides.narration: We now bring software engineering discipline to endpoint configuration. Instead of clicking through the portal and hoping you remember what you changed, you define configuration as versioned files, review them like code, and deploy them through automation. This lesson is about turning your Intune policies into something you can diff, review, and roll back.

slides.title: Why configuration as code?
bullets: The portal does not scale and leaves no history.
Declarative JSON files capture desired state.
Git gives audit trail, review, and rollback.
The repo is the source of truth, Intune the runtime.
slides.narration: Clicking through the Intune portal works for one device once. It does not scale, it leaves no history, and a single wrong click can hit thousands of endpoints. Configuration as code treats your desired state as declarative J S O N files, kept in Git and deployed by automation. You gain a diffable audit trail, peer review through pull requests, and rollback to any prior commit. The mental model is simple: the repo is the source of truth, and Intune is just the runtime that the repo deploys to.

slides.title: Export your current state
bullets: Capture what exists before changing anything.
Graph exposes policies as GET-able resources.
Serialise each to JSON with ConvertTo-Json.
Commit the folder as your baseline.
slides.narration: Always start by capturing what you already have. Graph exposes your configuration profiles as resources you can GET, and you serialise each one to J S O N with Convert To dash Json. Use a generous depth, like twenty, because these objects nest deeply and the default depth will silently truncate them. Write each policy to a file, commit that policies folder to Git, and now you have a baseline you can diff against forever. Never start config as code without first exporting the current state.

slides.title: Mind the JSON depth
bullets: ConvertTo-Json truncates at depth 2 by default.
Intune policies nest far deeper than that.
Use -Depth 20 to capture the whole object.
Round-trip and compare to verify nothing was lost.
slides.narration: A quick but critical warning. Convert To dash Json truncates at a depth of just two levels by default, and it does so silently. Intune policy objects nest far deeper than that, with settings inside settings inside instances. If you forget dash Depth, you will export J S O N that looks fine but is missing most of the policy. Always pass dash Depth twenty or more, and round trip your export, read it back and compare, to verify nothing was lost. This single flag catches a lot of people out.

slides.title: Idempotent import: create or update
bullets: The import must be safe to re-run.
Look up the policy by a stable key like name.
Update if it exists, create if it does not.
Run it twice; the second run changes nothing.
slides.narration: The heart of config as code is an import that is safe to re run. It looks the policy up by a stable key, usually the name, then updates it with a PATCH if it exists, or creates it with a POST if it does not. This is idempotency again, the same property we needed for remediations. The test is simple: run the import twice. The first run applies your change, and the second run should report no change at all. If a second run keeps creating duplicates, your import is not idempotent and needs fixing.

slides.title: Wrap it in a reviewable function
bullets: Function takes a policy file path.
SupportsShouldProcess gives -WhatIf preview.
PATCH on update, POST on create.
Same logic for every policy in the repo.
slides.narration: Wrap that create or update logic in a clean function that takes a policy file path. Add Supports Should Process so you get dash WhatIf for free, letting a reviewer or operator preview exactly what would change before it touches the fleet. The function reads the file, converts it from J S O N, looks for an existing policy by name, then PATCHes or POSTs. Because it is one function, you apply the identical logic to every policy in your repo by looping over the files.

slides.title: Separate templates from environment values
bullets: Never hard-code tenant or group ids in templates.
Keep environment values in a per-env file.
Inject them at deploy time.
Same template promotes dev to prod by swapping a file.
slides.narration: Do not hard code tenant or group ids inside a policy template. Keep those environment specific values in a separate parameter file, one per environment, and inject them at deploy time. Now the very same template promotes from dev to prod just by swapping which environment file you load. This is what stops the copy paste drift where your dev and prod policies slowly diverge until nobody knows what is actually deployed. Templates describe shape; environment files supply the specifics.

slides.title: The tooling landscape
bullets: Write your own, or use community tooling.
IntuneCM-style projects wrap export, import, assign.
Microsoft samples show the same patterns.
Principles are identical whatever you choose.
slides.narration: You can write your own importer, as we have here, or you can stand on existing community tooling. Projects in the Intune config manager family and Microsoft's own Graph samples wrap this whole export, import, and assign loop, adding backup and reporting on top. Whatever you choose, the underlying principles never change: declarative files as the source of truth, review through pull requests, and an idempotent deploy. Learn the pattern by hand first, then a tool just saves you typing.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Desired state lives in versioned JSON.
Export with -Depth, commit as baseline.
Idempotent import: create or update by name.
Keep environment values out of templates.
Task: build a minimal config-as-code pipeline by hand.
slides.narration: Let us recap. Configuration as code keeps your desired state in versioned J S O N, reviewed in Git and deployed by automation. Export your current policies with a generous dash Depth and commit them as a baseline. The import must be idempotent, create or update by name, so a second run changes nothing. And keep environment specific values out of your templates. Your task: export at least two configuration policies to J S O N and commit them, write an idempotent Import dash Intune Policy function with dash WhatIf, move a target group id out into a per environment file and inject it, then prove a second run reports no changes. See you in lesson six.
